title: Knowledge check: Changing Styles Through Classes

questions.prompt: Which principle best guides a correct implementation of changing styles through classes?
options: jQuery can read dimensions, positioning, scroll offsets, and computed CSS. Prefer classes and responsive CSS for presentation state, and avoid mixing layout reads with repeated writes.
Load multiple library copies and rely on whichever one executes last.
Skip error handling and assume the default browser state is always correct.
Render user-controlled strings as HTML so the browser can infer their meaning.
questions.answer_key: jQuery can read dimensions, positioning, scroll offsets, and computed CSS. Prefer classes and responsive CSS for presentation state, and avoid mixing layout reads with repeated writes.
questions.explanation: jQuery can read dimensions, positioning, scroll offsets, and computed CSS. Prefer classes and responsive CSS for presentation state, and avoid mixing layout reads with repeated writes. Apply this principle with the API/version documentation linked in the lesson.

questions.prompt: Which check is most useful after trying using css classes instead of inline styling?
options: Assume the first attempt succeeded and skip verification.
Use using css classes instead of inline styling deliberately, then inspect the actual DOM, request, or event result.
Use a removed jQuery API as the default for new code.
Bind another global handler after every render without cleanup.
questions.answer_key: Use using css classes instead of inline styling deliberately, then inspect the actual DOM, request, or event result.
questions.explanation: A focused observation checks behavior rather than assuming the method call guarantees the intended result. Include an edge case when the state or inputs can vary.

questions.prompt: Which verification approach best supports professional work with changing styles through classes?
options: Move answer keys and private configuration into frontend code.
Test only the first render and publish immediately.
Test a normal path and a relevant edge/failure path, and record expected versus actual behavior.
Replace all native browser APIs with jQuery whether needed or not.
questions.answer_key: Test a normal path and a relevant edge/failure path, and record expected versus actual behavior.
questions.explanation: Expected-versus-actual checks, relevant edge cases, and recorded limitations make the implementation easier to debug and review.
